CUTSA BAD-FAITH ATTORNEY'S FEE AWARDS (CIVIL CODE § 3426.4) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Bayline Roofing Services, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS CUTSA ATTORNEY'S FEE INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes the attorney's fee and cost provision of the California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, Civil Code section 3426.4, and the case law construing it. It sets out the three statutory circumstances in which a court may award fees and costs to the prevailing party in a trade secret misappropriation action (a claim made in bad faith, a motion to terminate an injunction made or resisted in bad faith, and willful and malicious misappropriation); the two-part definition of "bad faith" that the Courts of Appeal have adopted, requiring both objective speciousness of the claim and subjective bad faith in bringing or maintaining it (Gemini Aluminum Corp. v. California Custom Shapes, Inc.; FLIR Systems, Inc. v. Parrish; SASCO v. Rosendin Electric, Inc.; Cypress Semiconductor Corp. v. Maxim Integrated Products, Inc.); the kinds of evidence from which those courts have found each element; the rule that the provision reaches only claims about trade secrets and not claims about patents or trademarks (CytoDyn of New Mexico, Inc. v. Amerimmune Pharmaceuticals, Inc.); who counts as a prevailing party when a plaintiff voluntarily dismisses; the procedural rules that govern findings, hearings, appellate review, apportionment, and fees on appeal; and the parallel fee provision of the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act, 18 U.S.C. § 1836(b)(3)(D). It is prepared by Jordan T. Reyes concerning Bayline Roofing Services, Inc., in connection with an actual or potential trade secret dispute with Crestline Commercial Roofing, LLC and two former Bayline estimators involving the following claimed trade secret: The proprietary pricing model and supplier cost database used to prepare commercial roofing bids. This Information Sheet describes what the statute and the cited decisions say; it does not itself determine whether any claim is or was made in bad faith, whether any party is a prevailing party, or whether a court would award fees or costs in a specific dispute, and it is not a substitute for that case-specific legal determination.

THE STATUTORY TEXT: THREE TRIGGERS, A DISCRETIONARY AWARD TO THE PREVAILING PARTY, AND EXPERT WITNESS COSTS (CIV. CODE § 3426.4)
Civil Code section 3426.4 is the attorney's fee provision of the California Uniform Trade Secrets Act. It identifies three circumstances in which a court may award reasonable attorney's fees and costs to the prevailing party: when a claim of misappropriation is made in bad faith; when a motion to terminate an injunction is made or resisted in bad faith; or when willful and malicious misappropriation exists. The first circumstance operates in favor of a defendant who defeats a bad-faith claim, and the third operates in favor of a trade secret owner who proves willful and malicious misappropriation; the second can favor either side depending on who made or resisted the motion in bad faith. The award is discretionary ("may"), not mandatory. The section's second sentence, added by a 2006 amendment effective January 1, 2007, provides that recoverable costs under the section include a reasonable sum to cover the services of expert witnesses who are not regular employees of any party, actually incurred and reasonably necessary in preparation for or during trial or arbitration. The Court of Appeal in CytoDyn of New Mexico, Inc. v. Amerimmune Pharmaceuticals, Inc. summarized the section's place in the act: the act authorizes injunctions against actual or threatened misappropriation, allows recovery of actual loss and unjust enrichment, permits exemplary damages of up to double the damages award for willful and malicious misappropriation, and provides for attorney's fees in the three circumstances the section lists. The same court, in a footnote collecting cases decided under the section, described Vacco Industries, Inc. v. Van Den Berg (1992) 5 Cal.App.4th 34 as an award of fees to a plaintiff where two former employees and their company misappropriated protectible trade secrets and the jury found the misappropriation was done with malice, which illustrates the third trigger operating in a trade secret owner's favor.

THE PROVISION IS A DETERRENT TO SPECIOUS CLAIMS, AND AN AWARD UNDER IT IS A SANCTION WITHIN THE TRIAL COURT'S BROAD DISCRETION (GEMINI)
In Gemini Aluminum Corp. v. California Custom Shapes, Inc., the first published California decision to construe the term, the Court of Appeal observed that the act does not define "bad faith" and turned to a federal district court decision, Stilwell Development, Inc. v. Chen, which had examined the legislative history of section 3426.4. That history, as Gemini recounted it, shows the section was intended to allow a court to award reasonable attorney fees to a prevailing party in specified circumstances as a deterrent to specious claims of misappropriation. Gemini also characterized an award of attorney fees for bad faith as a sanction, and stated that the trial court has broad discretion in ruling on sanctions motions, so that a reviewing court accepts the version of the facts that supports the trial court's determination and indulges the inferences that favor its findings. In Gemini itself, the plaintiff had sued a former subcontractor for misappropriating the identity of a customer and die drawings for aluminum workbench parts; the jury rejected the plaintiff's related interference claim and, as an advisory matter, found the misappropriation claim was pursued in bad faith, and the trial court awarded the defendant $160,200 in fees after determining that at least 90 percent of its fees related to the misappropriation claim. The Court of Appeal affirmed. Later decisions repeat the deterrence rationale: FLIR Systems, Inc. v. Parrish states that section 3426.4 authorizes the trial court to award attorney fees as a deterrent to specious trade secret claims and that, because the award is a sanction, the trial court has broad discretion in awarding fees.

"BAD FAITH" HAS TWO ELEMENTS: OBJECTIVE SPECIOUSNESS (NOT FRIVOLOUSNESS) AND SUBJECTIVE BAD FAITH (GEMINI; FLIR)
Gemini adopted a two-part definition of "bad faith" for purposes of section 3426.4. The plaintiff in that case argued that the court should apply the standard of Code of Civil Procedure section 128.5, under which sanctions require conduct that is "frivolous" -- totally and completely without merit in the view of any reasonable attorney -- together with subjective bad faith. The Court of Appeal declined. It reasoned that section 3426.4 does not contain the word "frivolous," and that in enacting the section the Legislature was concerned with curbing "specious" actions for misappropriation, which may superficially appear to have merit. Finding the Stilwell analysis persuasive, the court held that "bad faith" under section 3426.4 requires objective speciousness of the plaintiff's claim, as opposed to frivolousness, and the plaintiff's subjective bad faith in bringing or maintaining the claim. FLIR Systems, Inc. v. Parrish restated the rule as a two-prong standard developed by the courts in the absence of a legislative definition: (1) objective speciousness of the claim, and (2) subjective bad faith in bringing or maintaining the action, meaning for an improper purpose. FLIR likewise rejected the argument that fees may not be awarded unless the action is frivolous under the section 128.5 standard. Both elements must be present; as the SASCO court later observed, prior courts opted to include an objective-speciousness element, thereby limiting a defendant's opportunity to recover fees to cases that are both objectively specious and subjectively brought in bad faith.

OBJECTIVE SPECIOUSNESS MEANS A COMPLETE LACK OF EVIDENCE; THE DEFENDANT NEED NOT PROVE A NEGATIVE (FLIR; SASCO; GEMINI)
The Courts of Appeal have given objective speciousness a concrete meaning. FLIR states that objective speciousness exists where the action superficially appears to have merit but there is a complete lack of evidence to support the claim. SASCO v. Rosendin Electric, Inc. applied that rule to a case in which an electrical contractor sued a competitor and three former senior managers on the theory that they must have taken its estimating and job-cost systems; the company's chief executive testified at deposition that he had no actual evidence the individuals took the documents and that "they either took it or they're stupid," and the plaintiff voluntarily dismissed without opposing a summary judgment motion. The Court of Appeal held that the defendants were not required to conclusively prove a negative -- that they did not steal the plaintiff's trade secrets -- and that under the objectively specious standard it was enough for the defendants to point to the absence of evidence of misappropriation in the record. It added that it was perfectly legitimate for the competitor to hire the individual defendants and for them to leave in favor of a competitor, and that speculation that departing employees must have taken trade secrets because they changed employers does not constitute evidence of misappropriation. Gemini illustrates a different route to speciousness: because a trade secret must derive independent economic value from not being generally known, a misappropriation claim lacks merit when the information has no independent economic value, and the Gemini plaintiff's claim was objectively specious from its inception because it was filed long after the customer's identity and the die drawings arguably held any value. Cypress Semiconductor Corp. v. Maxim Integrated Products, Inc. later remarked that the first clause of the FLIR formulation -- that the action superficially appear to have merit -- is superfluous, since there is no logical reason to require it.

THE OBJECTIVE INQUIRY ASKS WHETHER EVIDENCE EXISTS, NOT WHY IT IS MISSING; GENERAL SANCTIONS STATUTES ARE NOT IMPORTED (SASCO)
The SASCO plaintiff argued that the complete-lack-of-evidence rule should not apply to a case dismissed before trial and before the completion of discovery, especially where the defendants allegedly withheld discovery, and that the court should instead have applied the standard of Code of Civil Procedure section 128.7, under which a signer of a pleading represents that its factual contentions have evidentiary support or are likely to have it after a reasonable opportunity for investigation or discovery. The Court of Appeal declined. It reasoned that it makes no sense as a matter of statutory interpretation to insert a general pleading-abuse statute applicable to attorneys and others signing pleadings into a Civil Code section limited to the recovery of attorney's fees and costs in trade secret misappropriation claims; the two are separate remedies provided by the Legislature to address separate concerns through separate procedural mechanisms. The court noted that published cases had already rejected the Code of Civil Procedure section 128.5 frivolousness standard, and that the broader implication is that courts should apply the bad-faith standard of section 3426.4 in light of the purposes of the act rather than looking to nonapplicable sanctions statutes. It also rejected the argument that the defendants' alleged discovery misconduct should bear on the objective analysis: in determining whether there is a complete lack of evidence, a court should not ask why there is a complete lack of evidence. A plaintiff's explanation that it believed in its case and dismissed only because of the other side's discovery intransigence is an argument that goes solely to the subjective prong, where a court could find objective speciousness yet no subjective bad faith. The SASCO court further explained why the objective test is not whether it appeared at filing that discovery might turn up evidence: when an employee entrusted with trade secrets departs for a competitor, a reasonable observer might think discovery likely to unearth some support, but that predictive assessment has nothing to do with the plaintiff's good or bad faith, which is what the statute instructs courts to examine.

SUBJECTIVE BAD FAITH MEANS AN IMPROPER PURPOSE, WHICH IS USUALLY INFERRED FROM CIRCUMSTANTIAL EVIDENCE (SASCO; GEMINI; CYPRESS V. MAXIM)
The subjective element looks to the purpose for which the claim was brought or maintained. SASCO states that subjective bad faith under section 3426.4 means the action was commenced or continued for an improper purpose, such as harassment, delay, or to thwart competition, and that the absence of evidence alone, even after discovery, does not support a finding of subjective bad faith. Gemini, quoting earlier sanctions decisions, explained that good faith or its absence involves a factual inquiry into the plaintiff's subjective state of mind, that such a state of mind will rarely be susceptible of direct proof, and that the trial court will usually have to infer it from circumstantial evidence; it also noted that "bad faith" in this sense means simply that the action or tactic is being pursued for an improper motive. Cypress Semiconductor Corp. v. Maxim Integrated Products, Inc. clarified the relationship between purpose and belief: the test is not what the plaintiff believed about its objectively specious claim but for what purpose it pursued the claim, so that once a court finds a claim objectively specious and made for an improper purpose there is no further requirement that it also find a lack of subjective belief in the merits. The court acknowledged that a genuine belief in the merits tends to show a proper purpose and that a lack of such belief is strong evidence of an improper one, but held that a subjective belief in the merits does not bar a fee award where an objectively specious claim is found, on substantial evidence, to have been maintained for an improper purpose.

CIRCUMSTANCES FROM WHICH BAD FAITH HAS BEEN INFERRED: TIMING, PRESSING ON AFTER WARNINGS, AND BAD-FAITH MAINTENANCE OF A CLAIM BEGUN IN GOOD FAITH (GEMINI; FLIR)
The decisions identify recurring circumstances that support an inference of subjective bad faith. In Gemini, the timing of the action -- a misappropriation suit filed as what the trial court called a "knee-jerk response" to the defendant's small-claims collection action, long after the information could have had value -- raised an inference of bad faith. Gemini also adopted the principle that bad faith may be inferred where the specific shortcomings of the case are identified by opposing counsel and the decision is made to go forward despite the inability to respond to the arguments raised; there, the defendant had pointed out the claim's infirmities before trial, and the plaintiff's counsel replied that he did not want to reveal his theories or evidence, then argued at the fee hearing that the plaintiff had not attempted to prove the information was a trade secret. FLIR summarized these points: subjective bad faith may be inferred from evidence that the plaintiff intended to cause unnecessary delay, filed the action to harass, or harbored an improper motive; the timing of the action may raise an inference of bad faith; and similar inferences may be drawn where the plaintiff proceeds to trial after the action's fatal shortcomings are revealed by opposing counsel. FLIR also made explicit that the statute reaches maintenance as well as filing: sanctions may be awarded for the bad-faith filing or maintenance of a groundless action, and a trade secret claim could be brought in good faith but still warrant fees if pursued beyond the point where the plaintiff no longer believes the case has merit. FLIR added that a trial court awarding sanctions may consider a party's dilatory tactics and bad-faith settlement demands in maintaining the action.

AN ANTICOMPETITIVE MOTIVE AND A SUIT BUILT ON "INEVITABLE DISCLOSURE" SUPPORTED A $1.64 MILLION AWARD (FLIR)
FLIR Systems, Inc. v. Parrish affirmed a judgment and postjudgment order awarding two former executives $1,641,216.78 in attorney's fees and costs ($1,352,000 in fees and $289,216.78 in costs) after an eight-day permanent-injunction trial at which the court found no misappropriation or threatened misappropriation. The plaintiffs had sued when the executives announced plans to start a company to mass-produce microbolometers, on the theory that they could not do so on their planned timeline without misappropriating trade secrets; the defendants received no funding, started no business, and sold no products. The trial court found the action was brought in bad faith based on a theory of inevitable disclosure, a doctrine not recognized in California because it contravenes the state's strong public policy of employee mobility, and the Court of Appeal agreed that the doctrine is not the law in California. On the objective prong, the Court of Appeal pointed to the plaintiffs' chief executive's testimony, when asked why the action was filed, that the company could not tolerate a direct competitive threat by the two men; he had no evidence of wrongdoing but was bothered that they planned to compete in the future, and the evidence supported the finding that the plaintiffs filed a specious action as a preemptive strike and for an anticompetitive purpose. The court held that speculation that a departing employee may misappropriate and use a trade secret in a startup will not support an injunction, that mere possession of trade secrets by a departing employee is not enough, and that a post-filing discovery that one defendant had copied an unreadable database to a home hard drive, later destroyed, was not a threatened misappropriation. On the subjective prong, the court cited contradictory testimony by the plaintiffs' executives, who did not want to take responsibility for the suit and described the defendants as trustworthy; the plaintiffs' failure to identify what trade secrets would be covered by the proposed injunction; a proposed injunction that would have barred the defendants from developing certain products for twelve months even without using the plaintiffs' technology, which the court called an unlawful restraint on trade under Business and Professions Code section 16600 and strong evidence of subjective bad faith; and settlement demands for a payment, a noncompetition agreement, a no-hire promise, and silence toward the patent office, which the court found inflammatory, contrary to public policy, and made in bad faith.

SURVIVING SUMMARY JUDGMENT, NONSUIT, OR A MOTION IN LIMINE DOES NOT IMMUNIZE A PLAINTIFF FROM A BAD-FAITH FINDING (FLIR; GEMINI)
The FLIR plaintiffs argued that the trial court was estopped from finding bad faith because it had denied a motion for summary judgment, a motion in limine, and two nonsuit motions. The Court of Appeal acknowledged that in certain tort actions, such as malicious prosecution, the denial of summary judgment normally precludes a later finding that the lawsuit was frivolous, but noted that the rule is not absolute -- for example, where the denial was induced by materially false facts submitted in opposition. In FLIR, the plaintiffs had opposed summary judgment with expert declarations suggesting there was a scientific methodology for predicting the likelihood of trade secret misuse; the trial court, erring on the side of caution in a highly technical case, denied the motion to see what would develop; and at trial the same experts admitted there was no valid scientific methodology and agreed that no trade secrets were misappropriated. The Court of Appeal held that the plaintiffs cited no California authority that the denial of summary judgment in a trade secret case precludes the trial court from finding, after hearing all the evidence, that the action was brought or maintained in bad faith, and reasoned that if the rule were otherwise a trade secret plaintiff could file sham declarations to defeat summary judgment and immunize itself from sanctions. It relied on Gemini, which had rejected the argument that the denial of a nonsuit motion established a lack of bad faith; the Gemini court went so far as to say that, in its view, nonsuit should have been granted on the entire case. FLIR also rejected the argument that a tentative statement of decision finding the defendants had not proved an unclean-hands defense precluded a bad-faith finding, explaining that a tentative decision is not binding and that unclean hands concerns misconduct before the lawsuit was filed, not the bad-faith filing or maintenance of the action.

A DEFENDANT CAN BE THE PREVAILING PARTY WHEN THE PLAINTIFF VOLUNTARILY DISMISSES TO AVOID AN ADVERSE RULING (CYPRESS V. MAXIM; SASCO)
Section 3426.4 awards fees to the "prevailing party," and two of the leading decisions involved plaintiffs that dismissed their own actions. In SASCO, the plaintiff voluntarily dismissed after obtaining continuances of a summary judgment hearing and without ever filing an opposition; the trial court's finding that the defendants were prevailing parties was not challenged on appeal, and the Court of Appeal affirmed a fee and cost award of $484,943.46. In Cypress Semiconductor Corp. v. Maxim Integrated Products, Inc., the plaintiff dismissed without prejudice after losing an application for a temporary restraining order and a motion to seal, and while a demurrer to its amended complaint was pending; the trial court awarded the defendant $180,817.50 in fees, and the plaintiff argued on appeal that there was no prevailing party because it remained free to refile. The Court of Appeal identified three questions that application of the section naturally raises -- whether the defendant is the prevailing party, whether the claim was made in bad faith, and what fee is reasonable -- and rejected the argument that the trial court had mechanically applied the cost statute's definition of prevailing party. It observed that the risk of arbitrary results from a mechanical definition, which had led other courts to ask whether a party prevailed "on a practical level," will rarely arise under section 3426.4 because an award requires a finding of bad faith, so that the statute would seem to warrant a liberal construction of "prevailing party," trusting the bad-faith requirement to filter out doubtful cases. Without finally deciding that question, the court held that any reasonable finder of fact would find the defendant prevailed on a practical level: the plaintiff lost at every subsidiary stage, gained no legitimate benefit, and abandoned the action rather than face a merits determination that would certainly have been adverse, and the trial court could properly infer that the suit was dismissed to avoid an adverse adjudication. The defendant's brief stipulated standstill on soliciting the plaintiff's employees was nothing like the plaintiff's complete abandonment of its lawsuit and was not the injunction the plaintiff had prayed for.

A SUIT AIMED AT DETERRING A COMPETITOR'S LAWFUL RECRUITING OF EMPLOYEES WAS FOUND OBJECTIVELY SPECIOUS AND BROUGHT FOR AN IMPROPER PURPOSE (CYPRESS V. MAXIM)
Cypress Semiconductor Corp. v. Maxim Integrated Products, Inc. affirmed a bad-faith fee award against a plaintiff whose complaint accused a competitor of trade secret misappropriation for using a recruiter to solicit the plaintiff's touchscreen engineers. The Court of Appeal found the complaint meritless on its face: the only colorably actionable conduct attributed to the defendant was its attempt to recruit the plaintiff's employees, and, quoting long-standing authority, the court stated that no actionable wrong is committed by a competitor who solicits or hires away a competitor's employees who are not under contract, so long as the inducement to leave is not accompanied by unlawful action. The plaintiff's first theory -- that the defendant was "apparently" using improperly obtained confidential information to identify touchscreen employees -- was speculative on its face, and the defendant's attorneys demonstrated that nearly one hundred such employees could be identified from a professional networking website and patent records. The second theory -- that the defendant sought to hire the employees in order to extract trade secrets from them -- was, in the absence of any facts suggesting a threatened misappropriation, a de facto invocation of the inevitable disclosure doctrine, which courts in California have rejected. On improper purpose, the court relied on the plaintiff's presuit letters threatening to sue and to make the next hire "not cheap" for the competitor, which supported an inference that the purpose of the lawsuit was to impose a financial penalty upon, and thereby deter, the defendant's attempts to hire the plaintiff's technical employees; a press release issued on the day of dismissal announcing that the plaintiff would file again if it perceived further efforts to hire its employees; the plaintiff's belated and evasive response to the defendant's demand under Code of Civil Procedure section 2019.210 to identify the trade secrets at issue; and litigation tactics that magnified the defendant's expense, including amending the complaint on the last day to oppose a demurrer and an unsound motion to seal information the defendant had compiled from public sources.

THE PROVISION REACHES ONLY CLAIMS OF TRADE SECRET MISAPPROPRIATION, NOT CLAIMS ABOUT PATENTS OR TRADEMARKS (CYTODYN)
CytoDyn of New Mexico, Inc. v. Amerimmune Pharmaceuticals, Inc. reversed a $151,451.44 fee award because the plaintiff's complaint, though it used the word "misappropriation" repeatedly and prayed for exemplary damages under Civil Code section 3426.3, did not allege a claim for misappropriation of a trade secret. The complaint's causes of action -- inducement of breach of contract, unfair competition, fraud, and unjust enrichment -- were directed in substance to the alleged misappropriation of the plaintiff's patents and trademarks, and the phrase "trade secrets" did not appear in the body of the complaint except in one reference to a privilege assertion. The Court of Appeal explained that, as is obvious from the statute, the misappropriation for which a complainant may obtain relief under the act is solely confined to the misappropriation of a trade secret, and likewise the attorney's fees a prevailing party may obtain are for the malicious misappropriation of a trade secret or for a claim of misappropriation of a trade secret made in bad faith. Patents and marks are not trade secrets, and the misappropriation of patents and marks is not a subject with which the act is concerned; a complaint's erroneous, or even bad-faith, request for exemplary damages under the act does not convert the lawsuit into a trade secret claim, because the factual allegations control over the label given the pleading or the prayer for relief. The court did not disagree with the trial court's observations that no evidence supported the misappropriation allegations and that the plaintiff's conduct of the lawsuit evinced bad faith, but held that where statutory attorney's fees are concerned the trial court is constrained by the statute, as is the reviewing court. In short, the act does not authorize an award of fees when a claim of misappropriation of a patent or a trademark is made in bad faith; it applies only to trade secrets. The court also noted that the defendants' own answer had prayed for fees under Code of Civil Procedure section 128.7 rather than section 3426.4, and later decisions cite CytoDyn for the point that the two provisions are separate and unrelated.

THE FEDERAL DEFEND TRADE SECRETS ACT CONTAINS A PARALLEL FEE PROVISION (18 U.S.C. § 1836(B)(3)(D))
The federal Defend Trade Secrets Act, which created a federal civil cause of action for misappropriation of a trade secret related to a product or service used in interstate or foreign commerce, contains a fee provision that tracks the structure of Civil Code section 3426.4. In a federal civil action, a court may, if a claim of the misappropriation is made in bad faith -- which the statute expressly says may be established by circumstantial evidence -- or a motion to terminate an injunction is made or opposed in bad faith, or the trade secret was willfully and maliciously misappropriated, award reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing party. The federal text differs from the California text in three visible respects: it states on its face that bad faith may be shown circumstantially, a point the California courts reached through case law; it refers to a motion "opposed" rather than "resisted" in bad faith; and it speaks of attorney's fees without the California provision's express reference to costs and expert witness fees. The federal provision is interpreted by federal courts, and the California decisions construing "bad faith" under section 3426.4 are not themselves binding on the meaning of the federal text.

Civil Code section 3426.4 is the attorney's fee provision of the California Uniform Trade Secrets Act. It identifies three circumstances in which a court may award reasonable attorney's fees and costs to the prevailing party: when a claim of misappropriation is made in bad faith; when a motion to terminate an injunction is made or resisted in bad faith; or when willful and malicious misappropriation exists. The first circumstance operates in favor of a defendant who defeats a bad-faith claim, and the third operates in favor of a trade secret owner who proves willful and malicious misappropriation; the second can favor either side depending on who made or resisted the motion in bad faith. The award is discretionary ("may"), not mandatory. The section's second sentence, added by a 2006 amendment effective January 1, 2007, provides that recoverable costs under the section include a reasonable sum to cover the services of expert witnesses who are not regular employees of any party, actually incurred and reasonably necessary in preparation for or during trial or arbitration. The Court of Appeal in CytoDyn of New Mexico, Inc. v. Amerimmune Pharmaceuticals, Inc. summarized the section's place in the act: the act authorizes injunctions against actual or threatened misappropriation, allows recovery of actual loss and unjust enrichment, permits exemplary damages of up to double the damages award for willful and malicious misappropriation, and provides for attorney's fees in the three circumstances the section lists. The same court, in a footnote collecting cases decided under the section, described Vacco Industries, Inc. v. Van Den Berg (1992) 5 Cal.App.4th 34 as an award of fees to a plaintiff where two former employees and their company misappropriated protectible trade secrets and the jury found the misappropriation was done with malice, which illustrates the third trigger operating in a trade secret owner's favor.

FLIR states that objective speciousness exists where the action superficially appears to have merit but there is a complete lack of evidence to support the claim. SASCO v. Rosendin Electric, Inc. applied that rule to a case in which an electrical contractor sued a competitor and three former senior managers on the theory that they must have taken its estimating and job-cost systems; the company's chief executive testified at deposition that he had no actual evidence the individuals took the documents and that "they either took it or they're stupid," and the plaintiff voluntarily dismissed without opposing a summary judgment motion. The Court of Appeal held that the defendants were not required to conclusively prove a negative -- that they did not steal the plaintiff's trade secrets -- and that under the objectively specious standard it was enough for the defendants to point to the absence of evidence of misappropriation in the record. It added that it was perfectly legitimate for the competitor to hire the individual defendants and for them to leave in favor of a competitor, and that speculation that departing employees must have taken trade secrets because they changed employers does not constitute evidence of misappropriation. Gemini illustrates a different route to speciousness: because a trade secret must derive independent economic value from not being generally known, a misappropriation claim lacks merit when the information has no independent economic value, and the Gemini plaintiff's claim was objectively specious from its inception because it was filed long after the customer's identity and the die drawings arguably held any value. Cypress Semiconductor Corp. v. Maxim Integrated Products, Inc. later remarked that the first clause of the FLIR formulation -- that the action superficially appear to have merit -- is superfluous, since there is no logical reason to require it.

expectedJSON.body: The SASCO plaintiff argued that the complete-lack-of-evidence rule should not apply to a case dismissed before trial and before the completion of discovery, especially where the defendants allegedly withheld discovery, and that the court should instead have applied the standard of Code of Civil Procedure section 128.7, under which a signer of a pleading represents that its factual contentions have evidentiary support or are likely to have it after a reasonable opportunity for investigation or discovery. The Court of Appeal declined. It reasoned that it makes no sense as a matter of statutory interpretation to insert a general pleading-abuse statute applicable to attorneys and others signing pleadings into a Civil Code section limited to the recovery of attorney's fees and costs in trade secret misappropriation claims; the two are separate remedies provided by the Legislature to address separate concerns through separate procedural mechanisms. The court noted that published cases had already rejected the Code of Civil Procedure section 128.5 frivolousness standard, and that the broader implication is that courts should apply the bad-faith standard of section 3426.4 in light of the purposes of the act rather than looking to nonapplicable sanctions statutes. It also rejected the argument that the defendants' alleged discovery misconduct should bear on the objective analysis: in determining whether there is a complete lack of evidence, a court should not ask why there is a complete lack of evidence. A plaintiff's explanation that it believed in its case and dismissed only because of the other side's discovery intransigence is an argument that goes solely to the subjective prong, where a court could find objective speciousness yet no subjective bad faith. The SASCO court further explained why the objective test is not whether it appeared at filing that discovery might turn up evidence: when an employee entrusted with trade secrets departs for a competitor, a reasonable observer might think discovery likely to unearth some support, but that predictive assessment has nothing to do with the plaintiff's good or bad faith, which is what the statute instructs courts to examine.

expectedJSON.body: The subjective element looks to the purpose for which the claim was brought or maintained. SASCO states that subjective bad faith under section 3426.4 means the action was commenced or continued for an improper purpose, such as harassment, delay, or to thwart competition, and that the absence of evidence alone, even after discovery, does not support a finding of subjective bad faith. Gemini, quoting earlier sanctions decisions, explained that good faith or its absence involves a factual inquiry into the plaintiff's subjective state of mind, that such a state of mind will rarely be susceptible of direct proof, and that the trial court will usually have to infer it from circumstantial evidence; it also noted that "bad faith" in this sense means simply that the action or tactic is being pursued for an improper motive. Cypress Semiconductor Corp. v. Maxim Integrated Products, Inc. clarified the relationship between purpose and belief: the test is not what the plaintiff believed about its objectively specious claim but for what purpose it pursued the claim, so that once a court finds a claim objectively specious and made for an improper purpose there is no further requirement that it also find a lack of subjective belief in the merits. The court acknowledged that a genuine belief in the merits tends to show a proper purpose and that a lack of such belief is strong evidence of an improper one, but held that a subjective belief in the merits does not bar a fee award where an objectively specious claim is found, on substantial evidence, to have been maintained for an improper purpose.

expectedJSON.body: The decisions identify recurring circumstances that support an inference of subjective bad faith. In Gemini, the timing of the action -- a misappropriation suit filed as what the trial court called a "knee-jerk response" to the defendant's small-claims collection action, long after the information could have had value -- raised an inference of bad faith. Gemini also adopted the principle that bad faith may be inferred where the specific shortcomings of the case are identified by opposing counsel and the decision is made to go forward despite the inability to respond to the arguments raised; there, the defendant had pointed out the claim's infirmities before trial, and the plaintiff's counsel replied that he did not want to reveal his theories or evidence, then argued at the fee hearing that the plaintiff had not attempted to prove the information was a trade secret. FLIR summarized these points: subjective bad faith may be inferred from evidence that the plaintiff intended to cause unnecessary delay, filed the action to harass, or harbored an improper motive; the timing of the action may raise an inference of bad faith; and similar inferences may be drawn where the plaintiff proceeds to trial after the action's fatal shortcomings are revealed by opposing counsel. FLIR also made explicit that the statute reaches maintenance as well as filing: sanctions may be awarded for the bad-faith filing or maintenance of a groundless action, and a trade secret claim could be brought in good faith but still warrant fees if pursued beyond the point where the plaintiff no longer believes the case has merit. FLIR added that a trial court awarding sanctions may consider a party's dilatory tactics and bad-faith settlement demands in maintaining the action.

expectedJSON.body: FLIR Systems, Inc. v. Parrish affirmed a judgment and postjudgment order awarding two former executives $1,641,216.78 in attorney's fees and costs ($1,352,000 in fees and $289,216.78 in costs) after an eight-day permanent-injunction trial at which the court found no misappropriation or threatened misappropriation. The plaintiffs had sued when the executives announced plans to start a company to mass-produce microbolometers, on the theory that they could not do so on their planned timeline without misappropriating trade secrets; the defendants received no funding, started no business, and sold no products. The trial court found the action was brought in bad faith based on a theory of inevitable disclosure, a doctrine not recognized in California because it contravenes the state's strong public policy of employee mobility, and the Court of Appeal agreed that the doctrine is not the law in California. On the objective prong, the Court of Appeal pointed to the plaintiffs' chief executive's testimony, when asked why the action was filed, that the company could not tolerate a direct competitive threat by the two men; he had no evidence of wrongdoing but was bothered that they planned to compete in the future, and the evidence supported the finding that the plaintiffs filed a specious action as a preemptive strike and for an anticompetitive purpose. The court held that speculation that a departing employee may misappropriate and use a trade secret in a startup will not support an injunction, that mere possession of trade secrets by a departing employee is not enough, and that a post-filing discovery that one defendant had copied an unreadable database to a home hard drive, later destroyed, was not a threatened misappropriation. On the subjective prong, the court cited contradictory testimony by the plaintiffs' executives, who did not want to take responsibility for the suit and described the defendants as trustworthy; the plaintiffs' failure to identify what trade secrets would be covered by the proposed injunction; a proposed injunction that would have barred the defendants from developing certain products for twelve months even without using the plaintiffs' technology, which the court called an unlawful restraint on trade under Business and Professions Code section 16600 and strong evidence of subjective bad faith; and settlement demands for a payment, a noncompetition agreement, a no-hire promise, and silence toward the patent office, which the court found inflammatory, contrary to public policy, and made in bad faith.

expectedJSON.body: The FLIR plaintiffs argued that the trial court was estopped from finding bad faith because it had denied a motion for summary judgment, a motion in limine, and two nonsuit motions. The Court of Appeal acknowledged that in certain tort actions, such as malicious prosecution, the denial of summary judgment normally precludes a later finding that the lawsuit was frivolous, but noted that the rule is not absolute -- for example, where the denial was induced by materially false facts submitted in opposition. In FLIR, the plaintiffs had opposed summary judgment with expert declarations suggesting there was a scientific methodology for predicting the likelihood of trade secret misuse; the trial court, erring on the side of caution in a highly technical case, denied the motion to see what would develop; and at trial the same experts admitted there was no valid scientific methodology and agreed that no trade secrets were misappropriated. The Court of Appeal held that the plaintiffs cited no California authority that the denial of summary judgment in a trade secret case precludes the trial court from finding, after hearing all the evidence, that the action was brought or maintained in bad faith, and reasoned that if the rule were otherwise a trade secret plaintiff could file sham declarations to defeat summary judgment and immunize itself from sanctions. It relied on Gemini, which had rejected the argument that the denial of a nonsuit motion established a lack of bad faith; the Gemini court went so far as to say that, in its view, nonsuit should have been granted on the entire case. FLIR also rejected the argument that a tentative statement of decision finding the defendants had not proved an unclean-hands defense precluded a bad-faith finding, explaining that a tentative decision is not binding and that unclean hands concerns misconduct before the lawsuit was filed, not the bad-faith filing or maintenance of the action.

expectedJSON.body: Section 3426.4 awards fees to the "prevailing party," and two of the leading decisions involved plaintiffs that dismissed their own actions. In SASCO, the plaintiff voluntarily dismissed after obtaining continuances of a summary judgment hearing and without ever filing an opposition; the trial court's finding that the defendants were prevailing parties was not challenged on appeal, and the Court of Appeal affirmed a fee and cost award of $484,943.46. In Cypress Semiconductor Corp. v. Maxim Integrated Products, Inc., the plaintiff dismissed without prejudice after losing an application for a temporary restraining order and a motion to seal, and while a demurrer to its amended complaint was pending; the trial court awarded the defendant $180,817.50 in fees, and the plaintiff argued on appeal that there was no prevailing party because it remained free to refile. The Court of Appeal identified three questions that application of the section naturally raises -- whether the defendant is the prevailing party, whether the claim was made in bad faith, and what fee is reasonable -- and rejected the argument that the trial court had mechanically applied the cost statute's definition of prevailing party. It observed that the risk of arbitrary results from a mechanical definition, which had led other courts to ask whether a party prevailed "on a practical level," will rarely arise under section 3426.4 because an award requires a finding of bad faith, so that the statute would seem to warrant a liberal construction of "prevailing party," trusting the bad-faith requirement to filter out doubtful cases. Without finally deciding that question, the court held that any reasonable finder of fact would find the defendant prevailed on a practical level: the plaintiff lost at every subsidiary stage, gained no legitimate benefit, and abandoned the action rather than face a merits determination that would certainly have been adverse, and the trial court could properly infer that the suit was dismissed to avoid an adverse adjudication. The defendant's brief stipulated standstill on soliciting the plaintiff's employees was nothing like the plaintiff's complete abandonment of its lawsuit and was not the injunction the plaintiff had prayed for.

expectedJSON.body: Cypress Semiconductor Corp. v. Maxim Integrated Products, Inc. affirmed a bad-faith fee award against a plaintiff whose complaint accused a competitor of trade secret misappropriation for using a recruiter to solicit the plaintiff's touchscreen engineers. The Court of Appeal found the complaint meritless on its face: the only colorably actionable conduct attributed to the defendant was its attempt to recruit the plaintiff's employees, and, quoting long-standing authority, the court stated that no actionable wrong is committed by a competitor who solicits or hires away a competitor's employees who are not under contract, so long as the inducement to leave is not accompanied by unlawful action. The plaintiff's first theory -- that the defendant was "apparently" using improperly obtained confidential information to identify touchscreen employees -- was speculative on its face, and the defendant's attorneys demonstrated that nearly one hundred such employees could be identified from a professional networking website and patent records. The second theory -- that the defendant sought to hire the employees in order to extract trade secrets from them -- was, in the absence of any facts suggesting a threatened misappropriation, a de facto invocation of the inevitable disclosure doctrine, which courts in California have rejected. On improper purpose, the court relied on the plaintiff's presuit letters threatening to sue and to make the next hire "not cheap" for the competitor, which supported an inference that the purpose of the lawsuit was to impose a financial penalty upon, and thereby deter, the defendant's attempts to hire the plaintiff's technical employees; a press release issued on the day of dismissal announcing that the plaintiff would file again if it perceived further efforts to hire its employees; the plaintiff's belated and evasive response to the defendant's demand under Code of Civil Procedure section 2019.210 to identify the trade secrets at issue; and litigation tactics that magnified the defendant's expense, including amending the complaint on the last day to oppose a demurrer and an unsound motion to seal information the defendant had compiled from public sources.

expectedJSON.body: CytoDyn of New Mexico, Inc. v. Amerimmune Pharmaceuticals, Inc. reversed a $151,451.44 fee award because the plaintiff's complaint, though it used the word "misappropriation" repeatedly and prayed for exemplary damages under Civil Code section 3426.3, did not allege a claim for misappropriation of a trade secret. The complaint's causes of action -- inducement of breach of contract, unfair competition, fraud, and unjust enrichment -- were directed in substance to the alleged misappropriation of the plaintiff's patents and trademarks, and the phrase "trade secrets" did not appear in the body of the complaint except in one reference to a privilege assertion. The Court of Appeal explained that, as is obvious from the statute, the misappropriation for which a complainant may obtain relief under the act is solely confined to the misappropriation of a trade secret, and likewise the attorney's fees a prevailing party may obtain are for the malicious misappropriation of a trade secret or for a claim of misappropriation of a trade secret made in bad faith. Patents and marks are not trade secrets, and the misappropriation of patents and marks is not a subject with which the act is concerned; a complaint's erroneous, or even bad-faith, request for exemplary damages under the act does not convert the lawsuit into a trade secret claim, because the factual allegations control over the label given the pleading or the prayer for relief. The court did not disagree with the trial court's observations that no evidence supported the misappropriation allegations and that the plaintiff's conduct of the lawsuit evinced bad faith, but held that where statutory attorney's fees are concerned the trial court is constrained by the statute, as is the reviewing court. In short, the act does not authorize an award of fees when a claim of misappropriation of a patent or a trademark is made in bad faith; it applies only to trade secrets. The court also noted that the defendants' own answer had prayed for fees under Code of Civil Procedure section 128.7 rather than section 3426.4, and later decisions cite CytoDyn for the point that the two provisions are separate and unrelated.

expectedJSON.body: Several procedural rules emerge from the decisions. The burden on a section 3426.4 motion is on the party seeking fees: in Cypress Semiconductor Corp. v. Maxim Integrated Products, Inc., the Court of Appeal read the trial court's remark that a "fairly strict standard" had to be proved as a reference to the defendants, whose burden it was on the motion for fees to persuade the court that the action had been maintained in bad faith, and distinguished that burden from the plaintiff's burden of proof as plaintiff in the action. A trial court need not make express findings: Cypress v. Maxim rejected the argument that the trial court had made no finding on the subjective element, noting that the court had made no express finding but that prior authority had rejected the proposition that a court awarding fees under section 3426.4 must state the basis for its decision, and that a reviewing court presumes the trial court made all factual findings necessary to support the judgment for which substantial evidence exists. Because the subjective element may be proven or refuted by evidence that would have been wholly irrelevant at trial, FLIR (describing Yield Dynamics, Inc. v. TEA Systems Corp.) noted that it is error to exclude evidence proffered after trial that the action was filed in good faith; FLIR distinguished that case because the trial court there had not excluded evidence, had received voluminous briefing, and had already found objective and subjective bad faith, and the plaintiffs had neither objected to the briefing schedule nor offered proof of new evidence, so no further hearing was required. On appeal, an award will not be overturned in the absence of a manifest abuse of discretion, a prejudicial error of law, or necessary findings not supported by substantial evidence; the appellant, as FLIR put it, faces an uphill battle against both the sufficiency-of-evidence rule and the abuse-of-discretion rule, since the reviewing court does not retry cases or substitute its discretion for the trial court's. Cypress v. Maxim added that questions of law embedded in the ruling, such as the definition of "prevailing party," are reviewed independently.

expectedJSON.body: Because section 3426.4 authorizes fees only in connection with a claim of trade secret misappropriation, the decisions reflect apportionment where other causes of action were pursued alongside it. In Gemini, the trial court awarded $160,200 after determining that a minimum of 90 percent of the defendant's fees related to the misappropriation claim; in SASCO, the $484,943.46 award represented a discount on the total fees incurred to account for the non-trade-secret causes of action the plaintiff had pursued. The fee entitlement extends to appellate proceedings: Gemini held that fees recoverable under a statute are available for services at trial and on appeal, that the defendant as prevailing party on appeal was entitled to fees under section 3426.4, and that although the Court of Appeal has the power to fix fees on appeal, the better practice is to have the trial court determine them; it remanded for that purpose. SASCO and FLIR followed the same course, awarding the prevailing defendants their fees and costs on appeal in amounts to be determined by the trial court.

expectedJSON.body: The federal Defend Trade Secrets Act, which created a federal civil cause of action for misappropriation of a trade secret related to a product or service used in interstate or foreign commerce, contains a fee provision that tracks the structure of Civil Code section 3426.4. In a federal civil action, a court may, if a claim of the misappropriation is made in bad faith -- which the statute expressly says may be established by circumstantial evidence -- or a motion to terminate an injunction is made or opposed in bad faith, or the trade secret was willfully and maliciously misappropriated, award reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing party. The federal text differs from the California text in three visible respects: it states on its face that bad faith may be shown circumstantially, a point the California courts reached through case law; it refers to a motion "opposed" rather than "resisted" in bad faith; and it speaks of attorney's fees without the California provision's express reference to costs and expert witness fees. The federal provision is interpreted by federal courts, and the California decisions construing "bad faith" under section 3426.4 are not themselves binding on the meaning of the federal text.
